the claim and a critical discussion of the lack a behavioral correlation would be helpful; alternatively
the framing must shift to steady-state experience dependence rather than one-shot encoding.
We agree with the reviewer that the increased rate of BTSP-like events primarily on the first
day of learning suggests that this rate increase may be largely driven by novelty. We have removed
mentions of “one-shot learning” as it pertains to our findings. Additionally, we argue that the primary
novelty of our findings is the discovery of these BTSP-like events in a non-spatial task. Our
experiments were not designed to investigate the plasticity mechanism of BTSP itself, but rather to
characterize the phenomenon in a new context of non-spatial representations during expert
performance, which suggests that BTSP may underly the formation of other hippocampal
representations beyond place cells.
To disentangle the contribution of novelty and performance, we have reanalyzed the relevant
data. Rather than performing a simple correlation between rates of BTSP-like events and
performance, we now use a linear regression model that isolates the effect of day or performance on
the measure. We now display the t- and p-values associated with only the effect of performance for all
scatter plots (Figure 3d,e,g,h,I, Supplementary Figure S4f,g, and Supplementary Figure S6b,d,f,h).
Additionally, we include the results of each linear regression model in Supplementary Tables 1-11 to
demonstrate the relative effect of day, performance, and the interaction between the two factors.
Although there are changes from the originally displayed p-values, our overall conclusions about the
combined effect of day and performance are unaffected. We also include a more thorough discussion
of the new statistical approach and results.
Pooling of sample and test presentations
Combining encoding (sample) and retrieval/decision (test) odor epochs ignores distinct
neuromodulatory and network states, potentially conflating mechanisms that differ between
presentation positions. Separate analyses of event frequency, amplitude, success rate and field
selectivity for sample versus test are required—and pooling justified only if no significant differences
exist.
This is an important point as the first (sample) and second (test) odors could be encoded
differently in our CA1 neurons. We have added Supplementary Figure S4 (also included below) that
compares results when restricting analysis to either only the first or second odor. We find no
difference, which aligns with previous work in our lab studying odor representations in CA1 during the
same task (Figure S2 in (Taxidis et al., 2020)).
Detection analysis was re-run using either the first odors or second odor presentations. Complementing
previous work in the lab using the same task19, we find no difference between the two odors. a, Success rates
of small events are not different between first and second odors (paired t-test, p = 0.4342). Dots and lines
represent each animal (17 animals, which are the average for each of their 8 recording sessions). Error bars
represent the mean and SEM. b, Same as (a), but for ‘plateau-like’ events, which are also not different (paired t-
test, p = 0.2303). c, Similar to (a), but calculating the field time from reference as in Figure 1i for all newly
formed odor-fields (paired t-test, p = 0.2429). d, same as (c), but for ‘plateau-like’ events (paired t-test, p =
0.7371).
Unvalidated somatic proxy for dendritic plateaus
Equating somatic ΔF/F transients ≥10 SD with dendritic plateau potentials is unsubstantiated.
Electrotonic filtering blurs and attenuates distal events, and high-amplitude somatic bursts can
masquerade as plateaus. The authors should add direct measurements to support the claim of
dendritic integration and ideally provide tuft imaging or voltage recordings—or explicitly temper
mechanistic claims.
While our calcium imaging approach has some limitations, the restriction to somatic events is
not unique, and it aligns with previous spatial BTSP research that recorded ‘BTSP-like’ events using
somatic calcium imaging (Grienberger & Magee, 2022; Priestley et al., 2022; Sumegi et al., 2025).
The standard for measuring BTSP in place cell formation has been performing intracellular recordings
from somata and the main induction mechanism has been injecting current into the soma. In
Grienberger & Magee, 2022, a threshold of 3STD is used for CA1 place cell detection. Our use of
10STD is extremely conservative and limits analysis to only the very largest calcium somatic events
that likely propagate through most dendrites to many synapses (Milstein et al., 2021; Takahashi &
Magee, 2009). Furthermore, characterization of the BTSP-like events in Figure 1 is displayed across
a range of threshold values to demonstrate the relationship between event amplitude and odor field
measurements.
To address the reviewer’s point, we now refer to calcium events larger than 10STD to be
‘plateau-like’ events, and we have tempered mechanistic claims throughout the manuscript by
removing causal language. For example, we have replaced phrases such as “induction events drive
the formation of odor-fields” with “induction events precede the formation of odor-fields”. In the
Discussion, we also now discuss the challenge of understanding a theorized dendritic mechanism by
recording somatic events:
“Our somatic calcium imaging approach has the advantage of recording many neurons to find rare
‘BTSP-like’ events, but experiments to investigate dendritic dynamics will be valuable for further
understanding the underlying mechanisms of CA3 and EC inputs in driving BTSP. By focusing our
analysis to only the largest calcium events, we likely isolate events that propagate through most
dendrites to many synapses, but we recognize that some of these events may be large somatic
spiking bursts rather than those originating from dendritic plateau-potentials. Voltage and calcium
recordings of dendritic tufts at different depths with the stratum radiatum and stratum lacunosum-
moleculare will be necessary to evaluate the contributions of CA3 and EC inputs to the CA1 neurons.”
Incomplete reporting of event–field contingencies
Key denominators are missing: the number of large events that do not produce fields and the number
of fields arising without a detected event. Without a full contingency analysis and permutation or time-
shift controls, the strength and specificity of the event→field link cannot be assessed objectively.
denominators for key findings. We have clarified the text in the results section. We now state:
“We thus considered a reference calcium event as ‘plateau-like’ when its amplitude was > 10
STD. Plateau-like events were rare (122,605 out of 16,215,467 total events recorded = 0.76%) and
matched the shapes and amplitudes of previously described somatic calcium plateau events (Supp.
Fig. S3a-d). Approximately 8% of plateau like events that occurred during the odor cue or within the
ensuing 0.5 seconds preceded a subsequent odor-field formation (294 ‘successes’ out of 3876 total
events). This increased to ~15% during the second half of the odor presentation cue (Fig. 1j). Only 26
‘plateau-like’ events beyond 0.5 seconds after odor offset preceded a subsequent time-field formation
(8% of the 320 successful events). The odor-fields preceded by plateau-like events peaked 0.42 ±
0.14 seconds earlier in trial-time compared to the reference event (Fig. 1k). In contrast, only 0.28%
“small events” (<10 STD amplitude) during the odor cue or the ensuing 0.5 seconds (254 out of
91,635 total events) preceded new odor fields (Supp. Fig. S5a), These events represent the noise
floor of our detection criteria and the rare odor-field formation that formed without a preceding
‘plateau-like’ event. These rare fields were symmetrically distributed around the reference event
timepoint with increased variance (Supp. Fig. S5b). We thus label ‘plateau-like’ events preceding an
odor-field as ‘BTSP-like’. We observed no difference in success rates or asymmetrical field-formation
between first and second odor (Supp. Fig. S4). Therefore, all odor cues were pooled for further
analysis.”
Circular shuffle null mismatch and liberal thresholds for event detection
The “circular shuffle” null appears to include all odor windows (varying multiple odor trials depending
where in the trial number the event appeared (larger than 10, smaller than 90)—even those filtered
out of the real data—which violates exchangeability and likely biases p-values. Coupled with an
uncorrected 90th-percentile threshold (allowing up to 10% false positives per test) and no multiple-
comparison control, the field-significance method risks substantial type I error. A matched filtered null,
FDR correction, and simulation-based false positive rates are required.
We regret the misunderstanding caused by misleading language in our methodological details.
We have now improved our description of our Binary BTSP-like events detection, and state the
following:
“There were two criteria for an event to be considered a possible induction event: during the
previous 3 odor presentations the neuron must show no activity within 2 seconds before or after the
event in question, and there must not have been a firing field in the top 10% of shuffle data. To
determine the significance of a firing field, we took 6-second periods of all previous odor
presentations and found the peak of the average activity. We then circularly shuffled each odor
presentation and found the peak of the average activity from this shuffled data. This was repeated
2000 times to generate 2000 peak values from shuffled data. For a possible induction event, the real
peak of average activity must not have been greater than the 90th percentile of the shuffle.
This threshold was chosen to be extremely conservative by excluding all events that are preceded by
activity in the top 10% of shuffled data. If an event passed the previous criteria, we considered it as a
possible induction event. We then analyzed if it was successful in forming a field. There were four
criteria for a successful field formation: 1. The resulting field must have been significant above the
95th percentile of the shuffle; 2. The resulting field occurred within 2 seconds of the peak of the
induction event; 3. The neuron must have fired (have value above 2 STD) within 0.5 seconds of the
resulting field for the next 3 odor presentations; 4. The neuron must have fired within 0.5 seconds of
the resulting field for at least 7 out of the next 10 odor presentations. The strict criteria for activity in
the previous 3, following 3, and following 10 odor presentations improves the likelihood that the event
in question does induce a stable field. The ± 2 second window for the difference between the event
peak and field peak allowed us to look for asymmetrical formation without any bias. The lack of any
4
criteria regarding the amplitude of the induction event allowed us to probe the relationship of
amplitude to success rate and asymmetrical formation.”
One form of our analysis uses thresholds to split the induction events into two groups:
‘successes’ and ‘failures’. We based this analysis on previous published work on spatial BTSP
(Grienberger & Magee, 2022) and modified the criteria to fit our olfactory DNMS task with binary
categorization of odor-fields as in previous work in our lab using this task (Taxidis et al., 2020). Of
note, we made the criteria for detection of BTSP-like events even more conservative than this
previous study, since we can record from many more neurons.
We required the ‘possible induction event’ to have occurred within trials 11-90 because 10
trials before and after are needed for the analysis. No data is filtered out; we simply do not include
analysis of induction events that occur in the first or last 10 trials because we need 10 trials before
and after for our criteria. This requirement of trials before and after the induction event is consistent
with previous spatial BTSP research that exclude events in the beginning and/or end of recording
sessions (Grienberger & Magee, 2022; Sumegi et al., 2025). The 90th percentile threshold is used
only when finding possible induction events that occur after quiet periods without odor information.
We chose the 90th percentile as being more conservative than the 95th percentile because we
exclude from analysis all induction events that have an odor field greater than the 90th percentile in
the 10 trials preceding the induction event. Once an event passes criteria for being a possible
induction event with minimal activity in the preceding trials, we continue with a separate step for
determining odor field formation.
Our detection for odor field formation is very conservative as well. As compared to previous
analysis such as Grienberger and Magee, 2022, who only use 40% reliability in the following 5 trials,
we use a 95th percentile cutoff for the shuffle and also require 70% reliability in the following 10 trials.
Once again, the extremely minimal number of ‘successes’ from small events represent the baseline
level or noise floor for our analysis.
Despite our confidence in these conservative criteria, we agree that binarizing events is
inherently difficult and are dependent on threshold settings. While this binarized analysis is useful for
comparing our work with published spatial BTSP work, we recognize that non-binarized analysis is
also necessary. Therefore, we developed a threshold-free analysis in which we compare firing rate
increases across sets of trials before and after an induction event (Figure 1 L-N). We find a consistent
result across all possible sets of trials used for this analysis (Supplementary Figure S6 A-B). For all
experiments of learning and EC silencing, we include now both the binary event detection and
parameter-free firing rate increase measure.
Selective pre-exclusion of recent activity
Requiring no activity ±2 s in the three preceding odor presentations excludes neurons with ramping or
overlapping events, biasing the sample toward “clean” silent-to-active transitions. This pre-selection
may inflate apparent specificity and overlook biologically relevant induction contexts. The impact of
this filter must be quantified and, if necessary, replaced with a continuous covariate rather than binary
exclusion.
The binary event detection serves to demonstrate the rapid formation of odor-fields in a single
trial, aligning with the classic definition of BTSP and with previous BTSP research focused on large
somatic events preceded by laps with minimal activity. However, we agree with the reviewer that
setting thresholds binarizes the analysis. To address this, we developed the aforementioned
threshold-free firing rate increase measure where no pre-exclusion of recent activity is imposed.
Holographic induction paradigm limitations
reporting of total stimulation attempts or failure rates. The use of Kv2.1-targeted ChRmine biases
activation to proximal compartments, likely differing from natural tuft-driven plateaus. Negative
controls (sub-threshold, off-epoch, opsin-negative) and direct comparison of evoked versus
spontaneous event waveforms are essential before claiming sufficiency for field writing.
We agree that these optogenetic stimulations are likely different from naturally occurring
events; however, we attempted to replicate the standard in the spatial BTSP field, where current is
injected into the soma during whole-cell recordings to strongly depolarize the cell. The Kv2.1-targeted
ChRmine approach strongly depolarizes the soma in a similar way. In addition to the histograms of all
events, we have now included detailed numbers of attempts and successes in the results section. We
have now also included numbers of stimulation attempts that occurred outside the odor period and
when stimulation did not yield an observable calcium response (opsin-negative or non-responsive).
We find that only large calcium events > 10STD preceded odor field formation. No fields were formed
following weak responses, non-responses, or strong responses beyond one second after the odor.
Additionally, we now include a new supplementary figure (Supplementary Figure S3, also
included below) that compares the shapes and sizes of spontaneous and stimulated events. These
results align with other works characterizing template shape and size of somatic calcium events in
response to dendritic events (O’Hare et al., 2025). Our large somatic deconvolved events are
extremely rare, have larger and longer Delta F/F traces. Our optogenetic stimulation generated a
range of responses from 0 to 0.6 Delta F/F. The durations as measured by the full-width at half-
maximum of average traces were similar to spontaneously occurring events (between 1 and 1.5
seconds). The result section now states:
“Using these same criteria as above, we isolated stimulation events that were preceded by
minimal activity and no significant field (111 out of 857 total stimulations across 16 recording sessions
in 3 mice). Stimulation-induced ‘plateau-like’ events during the odor cue or ensuring 0.5 seconds had
an 11% probability of odor-field formation (5 out of 44 events), similar to that of spontaneous plateau-
like events (~8%). In contrast, stimulation-induced ‘plateau-like’ events outside of this time window (0
out of 33 events), or those with <10 STD amplitude (0 out of 34 stimulation attempts) were not
followed by field formation. Importantly, the success rate of field formation and firing rate increase
after stimulation (Fig. 2e-f) were similar to the spontaneous events we recorded in Figure 1.
Therefore, large somatic plateau-like events causally drive the formation of odor-fields similarly to our
observations of spontaneously occurring events.”

Absence of oscillatory-phase context
BTSP and dendritic excitability are known to be gated by theta phase. Without LFP recordings or
phase analysis, the role of rhythmic coordination is speculative. The authors should either provide
phase-locking data or explicitly limit mechanistic conclusions.

Limited odor set: Only two odors are tested. Generalization to richer odor spaces requires additional

scope of the current project which is to describe BTSP-like events outside of a spatial task. However,

Reviewer #2: Summary:
The study by Dorian et al. investigates whether behavioral timescale plasticity (BTSP) can drive the
formation of memory-related non-spatial hippocampal representations. This question is addressed by
performing calcium imaging from hippocampal CA1 cells as well as from LEC and MEC axons in CA1
while mice are performing an olfactory working memory task. In addition, optogenetic induction of
BTSPs in CA1 and chemogenetic manipulations of LEC and MEC are performed to establish that
the success and frequency of BTSPs. Furthermore, recordings during task acquisition show that the
relative frequency of BTSP is increased early in training on the odor task. The series of experiments is
performed with high rigor, and appropriate statistical methods are used. Importantly, the experiments
yield a highly novel result, which is that BTSP is a general plasticity mechanism and not limited to the
formation of spatial fields. In addition to reporting this key result, the study also characterizes some
mechanism of how BTSPs contribute to the encoding of non-spatial representations. As with any
novel phenomenon, the study of course raises a number of interesting questions for future work, such
as the limited effectiveness of BTSPs to generate fields later in the delay. The study is nonetheless
comprehensive as well as exceptional in its impact and novelty. There are only a few minor points
that, if addressed, would further improve the manuscript.
We thank the reviewer for their positive words and careful review of our manuscript. Overall, the
reviewer’s comments led to additional analysis and improved language that contribute to a stronger
manuscript.
Reviewer #2: Minor Points:
(1) The sentence in the abstract ‘Using holographic stimulation … ‘ is somewhat imprecise because
spontaneously-occurring events do not need stimulation.
We agree. We have adjusted this sentence in the abstract to say:
“Using two-photon calcium imaging of CA1 pyramidal neurons in mice learning an odor-cued working
memory task, we find spontaneously-occurring plateau-like calcium events during odor cues, forming
stable odor representations. These BTSP-like events were more frequent during early stages of task
learning, suggesting that BTSP is important for encoding novelty during learning. Additionally, using
holographic optogenetics, we induced plateau-like calcium events which were followed by stable odor
representations.”
(2) Fig. 1c. The blue bars are too small to be legible.
We have made the bars wider and brighter.
(3) Panels in Fig. 1g, S1 and S2 seem to show BTSP events later in the delay periods that do not
result in fields. Although the low effectiveness of these events to result in fields is pointed out in the
text, this could also be more explicitly labelled in the figure panels and mentioned in the figure
legends.
We have added an extra arrow in Figure 1g and described the ‘failures’ in the legends of each figure.
(4) Fig. 1i and S3. Although the results that small events rarely form odor fields is clear, it is less
obvious why the timing of the small events shows a value around zero distance from the reference
field. If these were completely random events there should at the minimum be an increase variance
because the event time and field time are unrelated. Is it possible that ‘small events’ correspond to an
odor fields that occur at a low rate, but nonetheless repeatedly around the same time? Perhaps this
point is so obvious that it is not explicitly mentioned. It would nonetheless be helpful for non-experts to
provide some explanation for the zero distance other than referring to randomness.
The reviewer raises an important point that we now clarify with the following statements in the Results
section:
“In contrast, only 0.28% “small events” (<10 STD amplitude) during the odor cue or the ensuing 0.5
seconds (254 out of 91,635 total events) preceded new odor fields (Supp. Fig. S5a), These events
represent the noise floor of our detection criteria and the rare odor-field formation that formed without
10
a preceding ‘plateau-like’ event. These rare fields were symmetrically distributed around the reference
event timepoint with increased variance (Supp. Fig. S5b).”
(5) Fig. 3 d, e, g and i, Fig. S4f and g, Fig. S6b, d, f and h. All the correlations with performance % (or
the lack thereof) seem to be a somewhat trivial consequence of effects occurring (or not occurring)
early in training. Performance is obviously lower early in training, and any effect that varies with
training days would thus necessarily also show a correlation with performance. If the question is
asked whether performance is a key predictor in addition to training days, one would have to do much
more sophisticated analysis than a simple regression. The relative effect of these two variables
(training day and performance) would need to be dissociated, for example by a partial correlation or
an analysis of variance that considers the relative contribution of each of the two factors (training day
and performance). Appropriate statistical methods should therefore be used, or all of the panels
plotting a variable against performance % should be removed along with the corresponding text.
We are thankful to the reviewer for their great suggestion. To disentangle the contribution of
novelty versus performance, we have reanalyzed the relevant data using a linear regression model
that is equivalent to an ANOVA with continuous variables. We can isolate the effect of day or
performance on each measure of BTSP-like events. We now display the t and p values associated
with only the effect of performance for all scatter plots (Figure 3d,e,g,h,I, Supplementary Figure S4f,g,
and Supplementary Figure S6b,d,f,h). Additionally, we include the results of each linear regression
model in Supplementary Tables 1-11 to demonstrate the relative effect of day, performance, and the
interaction between the two factors. Although there are changes from the originally displayed p-
values, our overall conclusions about the combined effect of day and performance are unaffected.
(6) The use of the term ‘odor axon’ for MEC axons can be somewhat misleading. While the activity of
these axons is clearly timed with regard to stimulus onset and offset, few have selectivity for a
particular odor. For comparison, we would not use the term ‘place cell’ if a cell were not selective for a
particular place.
We agree and have adjusted the figures and text to note axons that have their peak activity during the
1st odor, odor offset, or delay period. For example, the results section now states:
“A much higher percentage of MEC axons had significant peaks during odor presentations and their
offset compared to LEC axons (MEC with 28.0 ± 6.5% axons with activity peaking during odor
presentations compared to only 9.5 ± 6.5% for LEC; MEC with 4.6 ± 2.2% axons with activity peaking
during odor offset compared to only 2.7 ± 1.0% for LEC) (Fig. 5h). MEC axons with activity peaking
during odor presentations also showed greater trial reliability compared to LEC (Supp. Fig. S10d). In
contrast, a higher percentage of LEC axons had significant activity peaks during the delay period
(LEC with 5.8 ± 1.3% axons with activity peaking during delay period compared to only 2.4 ± 0.7% for
MEC).”
(7) The very last phrase in the Results section ‘being relayed indirectly through the CA1 perforant
path as well’ does not sound correct. First, the sentence seems to focus on LEC inputs, but the
perforant path through DG and CA3 would be conveying merged MEC and LEC inputs. Second, there
is no perforant path with a direct connection to CA1 and the meaning of a ‘CA1 perforant path’ is
therefore not evident.
We fixed the error in the wording to state “… being relayed indirectly to the CA1 via the perforant path
as well”
11
(8) In the Results and in the Discussion, it would be more precise to distinguish two potential types of
effects as a consequence of manipulating entorhinal inputs to CA1. One type is plasticity/BTSP-
related, and although detectable in well-trained mice, may no longer be as behaviorally relevant as it
would be if the manipulation were done earlier in training. The second type are effects on
hippocampal activity patterns as a consequence of loss of information from LEC or MEC. With any
manipulation of a brain region, effects on plasticity and from loss of inputs to connected circuits can
often not be fully dissociated. It is nonetheless important to conceptually distinguish between these
types of effects and to acknowledge that both contribute to differences in neuronal firing patterns
during/after manipulations.
We now discuss the difficulty of teasing these two potential effects apart in the Results:
“Collectively, LEC inhibition strongly decreased odor-selectivity and decodability in pyramidal CA1
neurons, which may have played a role in the reduction in the success rate of ‘plateau-like’ events in
generating odor-fields, though additional mechanisms could potentially contribute to this effect.
Additionally, these results are limited to expert performance, so we are unable to determine if these
manipulations would affect the previously found novelty and learning results.”
We discuss it in more detail in the Discussion:
“First, it is important to note that we only observed these effects in expert-performance. Perhaps the
effects that we observed in expert animals would become behaviorally relevant during early training.
Alternatively, the loss of information from LEC or MEC may affect CA1 activity regardless of the stage
of behavioral performance. Future experiments will be necessary to tease apart these possibilities.”

Reviewer #1:
Thank you for the detailed rebuttal and substantial revisions. Several of my earlier concerns are now
at least partially addressed, especially the change in terminology to “plateau-like” events, the added
discussion of somatic imaging caveats, and the corrections to error bars. However, I still feel that the
strength and scope of the main claims exceed what the data can support, and I would strongly
encourage further tempering of the mechanistic and causal language, as well as clearer
acknowledgment of alternative interpretations.
We thank the reviewer for their thoughtful feedback. We have now addressed these concerns
by improving our statistical tests and further tempering mechanistic and causal language while more
clearly discussing alternative interpretations of our results.
Mechanistic and causal claims
While the authors have removed some explicit causal phrases and now refer to “plateau-like” rather
than “BTSP-like” events, the title, abstract, and discussion still largely present the results as
demonstrating that BTSP is a general plasticity mechanism for non-spatial representations. In
particular, the concluding statement in the abstract that the findings “demonstrate a causal role of
BTSP” is not supported by the present data. Given that all inferences are based on somatic calcium
signals and an operational definition of ≥10 SD events, this remains too strong. The same somatic
signature could arise from different underlying mechanisms (e.g. bursts, mixed dendritic/somatic
events), and the data demonstrate correlation and temporal precedence rather than necessity or
sufficiency. I would recommend consistently rephrasing to something more neutral, such as “rare,
large somatic calcium events consistent with BTSP models can precede the formation of some odor
fields in this task,” and avoiding language that implies that BTSP per se has been established as the
mechanism.
We have made several changes to address these concerns.
First, we have changed the Title to read: “Rapid formation of non-spatial hippocampal
representations consistent with behavioral timescale synaptic plasticity is modulated by entorhinal
input”
Second, we have changed the concluding sentence in the Abstract to read: “Together, our
findings demonstrate that rare large somatic calcium events, consistent with BTSP, precede and drive
novel odor representations during learning, in a manner differentially regulated by medial and lateral
entorhinal cortex.”
Third, to be consistent with this new language, we have also adjusted similar summarizing
sentences in the Discussion.
Last, while we agree that tempering claims is appropriate in regard to the mechanism
underlying the formation of odor representations, we would like to point out that experimental results
shown in Figure 2 suggest sufficiency since we were able to optogenetically-induce odor
representations with somatic excitation. We now acknowledge that BTSP is likely just one of several
mechanisms potentially driving formation of hippocampal representations. Furthermore, we now more
fully discuss the difficult problem of testing necessity of BTSP in the Discussion.
The revised text better documents numerators/denominators and threshold choices, but the core
concern about circularity remains. “Possible induction events” are defined using stringent criteria (low
prior activity, no strong field in the preceding trials, restricted trial window), and “success” is then
defined as a new, reliable field emerging near the event in time. This effectively preselects events in
which a silent-to-active transition occurs with the desired temporal asymmetry and discards cases
where fields emerge more gradually, overlap existing activity, or arise without a qualifying event. The
binary analysis therefore builds the BTSP-like pattern into the inclusion criteria and will, by
construction, emphasize one-shot, asymmetric field formation. The more continuous “threshold-free”
analysis is a welcome addition, but the manuscript should more clearly acknowledge that the
binary/“induction” analysis is conditional on these strong filters and cannot be taken as an unbiased
estimate of how often plateau-like events genuinely drive fields versus other scenarios.
We have now further revised the text to emphasize the differences between the two types of
analysis. In the Results (page 4), it now reads “Categorizing BTSP-like events into successes and
failures restricted analysis to a narrowly defined type of plasticity event based on formation of
significant odor responses. Some responses were reinforced by multiple ‘plateau-like’ events (Supp.
Fig. S2). Therefore, we developed a simpler analysis to avoid artificially imposed criteria and
sensitivity to binary thresholding.”
In the Discussion, it now reads “analysis that binarizes complex dynamics into successes and
failures is sensitive to chosen thresholds, and this makes it inherently difficult to compare across
contexts and recording methods. Similar discrepancies can even be seen within spatial tasks, as the
reported percentages of CA1 pyramidal neurons that are classified as place cells can vary
dramatically between 20% and 90%50. Therefore, our reported values for BTSP success cannot be
extrapolated to BTSP rates beyond our experimental and analytical parameters. For this reason, we
also developed and utilized the threshold-free analysis of firing rate increase.”
As before, we argue that the binary analysis is still useful because of its widespread use in
spatial BTSP research classifying the formation of place fields, but we have now tempered our
explanations in the Results and Discussion.
Generality and time representations
The manuscript still suggests that BTSP underlies non-spatial representations more broadly, including
time. However, the data show that only a very small minority of plateau-like events occurring after
odor offset precede time fields, and optogenetic induction in the delay period did not reliably generate
fields. The discussion now notes that delay-related effects are weaker and rare, but the claims about
generalization to time and “internally generated” codes still read as if they are an established
extension of the mechanism rather than an open question. I would recommend explicitly stating that
the present data provide only limited support for BTSP-like contributions to time fields and that the
role of such events in temporal coding remains unresolved.
We agree with the reviewer. The noted section in the Discussion now reads “Although we
observed small firing rate increases and rare BTSP-like events that form odor-specific fields during
the delay period, our findings only provide limited support of BTSP-like events contributing to
temporal coding. Future studies should investigate if recurrent CA3 networks capable of generating
temporal codes55–57 can be activated coincidentally with LEC and MEC to drive BTSP for internally
generated representations.”
Behavioral relevance and EC silencing
odor decoding in CA1, but have no detectable effect on behavioral performance in the expert animals.
This is now documented more clearly, but the manuscript still leans toward a causal interpretation in
which BTSP-dependent representations are central for task solution. Given the lack of behavioral
effect in the regime actually recorded, a more balanced formulation would be that LEC and MEC
manipulations alter neural representations and event statistics during expert performance, but their
necessity for behavior under these conditions is not demonstrated. Any stronger inference about
“BTSP creating behaviorally relevant representations” should be softened accordingly or explicitly
framed as a hypothesis for future work (e.g. during acquisition or more demanding variants of the
task).
We have removed statements that mention ‘behavioral relevance’ in the Results and
Discussion. Additionally, we have expanded the section in the Discussion to further discuss this
important idea: “Perhaps the effects that we observed in expert animals would be stronger if tested
during early training. Alternatively, the loss of information from LEC or MEC may affect CA1 activity
regardless of the stage of behavioral performance. Furthermore, the lack of behavioral performance
deficits with either LEC or MEC inhibition suggests that these representations are not necessary for
the performance of this specific task. Future experiments with inhibition at different stages of learning
and across various tasks will be necessary to isolate the behavioral relevance of LEC and MEC
inputs driving BTSP-like events in CA1.”
Statistical issues
- The authors state that they now use linear regression to separate day and performance, and
they have corrected the chemogenetic error bars, which is appreciated. Nonetheless, several
statistical concerns remain:
- Regression analyses treat each animal–day as an independent data point without modeling
mouse as a random effect. With only five mice followed over multiple days, this violates the
hierarchical structure of the data and likely underestimates uncertainty on day/performance
effects.
We thank the reviewer for pointing out this error and have now updated all regression figures,
statistics, and supplemental tables after modeling mouse as a random effect (slope and intercept).
This approach is better suited to repeated measurements for each mouse, better captures animal
variability, has more power, and thus strengthens our findings. All corresponding figure panels now
display larger t-values and smaller p-values, including ‘Plateau-like’ Event Rate in Figure 3D which
is now significant but weaker than all other effects. We now note this difference in the text.
Supplemental Tables contain all MATLAB Table outputs regarding the model and results.
- Event-level analyses still appear to treat individual events as independent observations in
some tests, even though many events come from the same cells and animals, again inflating
effective n and p-values.
The reviewer’s point applies to Figures 1K and 2D depicting histograms for visualization. All
statistics and other figure panels are performed on animal averages or session averages. We
denote this in the legend text with statements such as “Individual thin gray lines represent each of
the 17 animals (which are the average for each of their 8 recording sessions)”. The only other use
of individual events is when we summarize total counts in the main text (e.g. “294 ‘successes’ out
of 3876 total events”), which are summary quantifications without statistics involved.
- The multi-factor ANOVAs in the chemogenetic experiments are based on very small group
sizes (e.g. n = 3 controls), where parametric assumptions are fragile and effect sizes or
confidence intervals would be more informative than marginal p-values.
about effect robustness and for avoiding strong mechanistic or causal claims based on borderline
statistics.
We appreciate this suggestion. In each figure legend corresponding to figure panels with three-way
ANOVAs we have now included the 95% confidence interval for each significant difference. This is
included for Figure 4B, 4C, 4E, 4F, 4G, 4I, and Supplementary Figure S6I.
Context from Sumegi et al.
The authors now cite Sumegi et al. as using somatic calcium to study BTSP-like phenomena.
Importantly, that work also shows that large somatic Ca² events with BTSP-like signatures are
neither necessary nor sufficient for place field formation and that diverse calcium dynamics can
underlie new fields. This does not contradict the present ⁺study, but it reinforces the idea that large
somatic “plateau-like” events are one of several possible routes to field formation. In my view, this
makes it even more important that the current manuscript frame its main conclusion as the
identification of one correlated pathway in a specific non-spatial task, rather than as establishing
BTSP as the general mechanism for non-spatial representations.
We have edited the first summary paragraph of the Discussion to read “These events are
consistent with models of behavioral timescale synaptic plasticity (BTSP), as they demonstrate
asymmetrical formation observed previously during spatial tasks1–11. This suggests that BTSP may be
one plasticity mechanism capable of driving rapid formation of hippocampal representations during
both spatial and non-spatial cognition.”
Additionally, we have expanded a section to discuss the diversity of calcium events as seen in
Sumegi et al. It now reads “Additionally, alternative mechanisms may also play a role, consistent with
recent research demonstrating a variety of somatic calcium dynamics preceding formation of place
fields51. Indeed, the rapid formation of odor responses after optogenetically-induced somatic plateau-
like events suggests sufficiency, but the low success rate suggests other mechanisms could also be
involved. Furthermore, tests of necessity are difficult due to our present limited knowledge of the
mechanisms underlying BTSP.”
In summary, the additional analyses and revisions improve the manuscript, but I still recommend a
further toning down of mechanistic and causal language, more explicit discussion of alternative
mechanisms and the limitations of the operational definition, clearer acknowledgment of the lack of
behavioral impact of EC silencing under the conditions tested, and a more cautious treatment of
generalization to time fields.
We thank the reviewer for their suggestions. We have addressed each of these concerns with
revisions of text throughout the Abstract, Results, and Discussion sections.
4

Thank you for the detailed rebuttal and substantial revisions. Several of my earlier concerns are now at least partially addressed, especially the change in terminology to “plateau-like” events, the added discussion of somatic imaging caveats, and the corrections to error bars. However, I still feel that the strength and scope of the main claims exceed what the data can support, and I would strongly encourage further tempering of the mechanistic and causal language, as well as clearer acknowledgment of alternative interpretations.
Mechanistic and causal claims
While the authors have removed some explicit causal phrases and now refer to “plateau-like” rather than “BTSP-like” events, the title, abstract, and discussion still largely present the results as demonstrating that BTSP is a general plasticity mechanism for non-spatial representations. In particular, the concluding statement in the abstract that the findings “demonstrate a causal role of BTSP” is not supported by the present data. The same somatic signature could arise from different underlying mechanisms (e.g. bursts, mixed dendritic/somatic events), and the data demonstrate correlation and temporal precedence rather than necessity or sufficiency. I would recommend consistently rephrasing to something more neutral, such as “rare, large somatic calcium events consistent with BTSP models can precede the formation of some odor fields in this task,” and avoiding language that implies that BTSP per se has been established as the mechanism.

The revised text better documents numerators/denominators and threshold choices, but the core concern about circularity remains. “Possible induction events” are defined using stringent criteria (low prior activity, no strong field in the preceding trials, restricted trial window), and “success” is then defined as a new, reliable field emerging near the event in time. This effectively preselects events in which a silent-to-active transition occurs with the desired temporal asymmetry and discards cases where fields emerge more gradually, overlap existing activity, or arise without a qualifying event. The binary analysis therefore builds the BTSP-like pattern into the inclusion criteria and will, by construction, emphasize one-shot, asymmetric field formation. Generality and time representations
The manuscript still suggests that BTSP underlies non-spatial representations more broadly, including time. However, the data show that only a very small minority of plateau-like events occurring after odor offset precede time fields, and optogenetic induction in the delay period did not reliably generate fields. The discussion now notes that delay-related effects are weaker and rare, but the claims about generalization to time and “internally generated” codes still read as if they are an established extension of the mechanism rather than an open question. I would recommend explicitly stating that the present data provide only limited support for BTSP-like contributions to time fields and that the role of such events in temporal coding remains unresolved.
Behavioral relevance and EC silencing
The chemogenetic manipulations clearly modulate plateau-like event rates, success probabilities, and odor decoding in CA1, but have no detectable effect on behavioral performance in the expert animals. This is now documented more clearly, but the manuscript still leans toward a causal interpretation in which BTSP-dependent representations are central for task solution. Given the lack of behavioral effect in the regime actually recorded, a more balanced formulation would be that LEC and MEC manipulations alter neural representations and event statistics during expert performance, but their necessity for behavior under these conditions is not demonstrated. Any stronger inference about “BTSP creating behaviorally relevant representations” should be softened accordingly or explicitly framed as a hypothesis for future work (e.g. during acquisition or more demanding variants of the task).

- The authors state that they now use linear regression to separate day and performance, and they have corrected the chemogenetic error bars, which is appreciated. Nonetheless, several statistical concerns remain:

- The multi-factor ANOVAs in the chemogenetic experiments are based on very small group sizes (e.g. n = 3 controls), where parametric assumptions are fragile and effect sizes or confidence intervals would be more informative than marginal p-values.

Context from Sumegi et al.
The authors now cite Sumegi et al. as using somatic calcium to study BTSP-like phenomena. Importantly, that work also shows that large somatic Ca²⁺ events with BTSP-like signatures are neither necessary nor sufficient for place field formation and that diverse calcium dynamics can underlie new fields. review_generation.input:
You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications, one of the world's leading multidisciplinary journals.

Read the following paper carefully and write a thorough, technically rigorous peer review. Identify the most important scientific concerns regarding: methodology, statistical analysis, data quality, claims vs. evidence, reproducibility, and clarity. Organise your review with clear sections.

## Abstract

Behavioral timescale synaptic plasticity (BTSP) is a form of synaptic potentiation where a single plateau potential in hippocampal neurons forms a place field during spatial learning. However, it remains unknown whether BTSP also forms non-spatial responses and what roles the medial and lateral entorhinal cortex (MEC and LEC) play in driving non-spatial BTSP. Using two-photon calcium imaging of CA1 pyramidal neurons in mice learning an odor-cued working memory task, we observed spontaneously-occurring large plateau-like calcium events during odor cues, forming stable odor representations. Using holographic optogenetics, we induced similar plateau-like calcium events in single neurons that were followed by novel odor representations. Chemogenetic inhibition of MEC reduced the frequency of plateau-like events, whereas LEC inhibition reduced their efficiency in forming odor representations. Together, our findings demonstrate that rare large somatic calcium events, consistent with BTSP, precede and drive novel odor representations in a manner differentially regulated by medial and lateral entorhinal cortex.

---

## Introduction

In many situations, learning is not a gradual process. In fact, our ability to make associations after a single experience is critical for survival. In the hippocampus, a region recognized for its importance in learning and memory, behavioral timescale synaptic plasticity (BTSP) has emerged as a robust mechanism for the rapid generation of spatial representations (place fields) following the occurrence of plateau potentials1–11. However, the hippocampus not only represents the location of animals in space12–15, but also non-spatial sensory information16–19. The hippocampus dynamically links these sensory experiences across time through sequential firing that tracks the passage of time after specific events14,19–22. It is unclear whether BTSP also plays a role in the formation of non-spatial sensory-driven or internally generated hippocampal representations.

Hebbian plasticity mechanisms such as spike-timing dependent plasticity require causality and many repetitions to potentiate synapses when presynaptic spikes precede postsynaptic action potentials by a few milliseconds23–26. While this mechanism may play a role in modulating hippocampal responses, BTSP has many features which could make it a more robust and rapid mechanism for the generation of non-spatial receptive fields. During spatial learning tasks, a single calcium plateau potential can serve as the induction event, asymmetrically boosting synaptic inputs that occur up to several seconds before the induction event, leading to a membrane potential ramp and reliable spatial firing on subsequent trials2,5,6. It is not known whether plateau potentials occurring during non-spatial tasks could also boost synaptic inputs at specific timepoints in the task leading to the rapid formation of stable representations of sensory stimuli and time. The rapid induction of these non-spatial hippocampal representations by BTSP could form the basis for rapid learning in the hippocampus.

The role of the entorhinal cortex (EC) in inducing BTSP events7 and relaying sensory information during non-spatial tasks18,27,28 is poorly understood. CA1 receives direct layer III EC input via the temporammonic (TA) pathway and indirect input via the perforant path from layer II EC to dentate gyrus (DG). DG then projects to CA3, which in turn projects to CA129,30. Lateral and medial EC (LEC and MEC) have distinct inputs and behaviorally relevant response properties: LEC robustly represents olfactory information31–34, while MEC mainly encodes visuo-spatial information35–38. Furthermore, the MEC plays a major role in the induction of plateau potential ‘teaching signals’ during BTSP induced during spatial learning tasks7. Yet, whether MEC and LEC play distinct roles in the generation of BTSP during non-spatial tasks remains to be determined.

To address these questions, we investigated multimodal representations within CA1 and EC during a non-spatial olfactory delayed non-match-to-sample (DNMS) working memory task19. We have previously shown that CA1 pyramidal neurons fire sequentially in response to specific odors and across the 5-second delay period during DNMS performance19. We hypothesized that non-spatial BTSP can generate odor representations in CA1 and that this process would be modulated by MEC and LEC inputs. Using two-photon calcium imaging of dorsal CA1, we recorded non-spatial ‘BTSP-like’ events; large somatic calcium ‘plateau-like’ events that preceded formation of odor-specific fields in CA1 during expert performance of the DNMS task. Combining this approach with holographic optogenetic stimulation, we successfully generated odor-specific representations in individual cells following a single stimulation. Recording dorsal CA1 across learning of the task revealed higher rates of BTSP-like events during the first day of learning compared to all subsequent days. In addition, we found that MEC chemogenetic inhibition decreased the frequency of large calcium induction events in CA1, while LEC inhibition reduced the success rate of odor-field generation. Finally, two-photon calcium imaging of temporammonic EC axonal projections to CA1 demonstrated that MEC axonal strong firing to odor presentations likely plays a role in driving large plateau-like calcium events in CA1, while LEC axonal odor-selectivity mediates plasticity in the formation of odor-fields after the large calcium induction event. Therefore, non-spatial ‘BTSP-like’ events form odor-fields during working memory performance and are differentially modulated by lateral and medial entorhinal cortex inhibition.

## Results

We used in vivo two-photon calcium imaging to record the activity of neurons in the pyramidal layer of dorsal CA1 while animals performed an olfactory delayed non-match-to-sample (DNMS) working memory task (Fig. 1a-e). Adult male and female mice (n=17) were injected with AAV1-Syn-jGCaMP8f into the right dorsal CA1 and implanted with a 3mm diameter glass-bottomed titanium cannula above the intact alveus after aspiration of the overlying cortex and corpus callosum19 (Fig. 1d-e). After one week of recovery, mice were water-restricted and trained on the olfactory DNMS working memory task19,39, while head-fixed on a spherical treadmill (Fig. 1a-b). Each trial consisted of two 1-second odor presentations separated by a 5-second delay period. One second after the offset of the 2nd odor, there was a 3-second reward period during which the choice of the animal was determined. Mice were trained to lick the lickport to release water during this reward period if the two odors did not match (correct ‘hit’). Mice learned to refrain from licking the lickport if the odors matched (correct ‘rejection’), and overall performance was quantified as the percentage of correct ‘hits’ and correct ‘rejections’ out of all trials. We considered performance above 85% to be expert level. Each session of the DNMS task consisted of 5 blocks of 20 trials, with pseudorandomly distributed odor combinations (Fig 1c). Mice were recorded for 8 days during expert performance for a total of 136 recording sessions yielding an average of 312 ± 125 (mean ± standard deviation) active neurons per day. We successfully imaged the same field of view (FOV) for each of the 8 days for all animals. Calcium signals were extracted and deconvolved using Suite2p40 (see methods).

Non-spatial BTSP-like events in CA1 formed stable odor-specific fields

In our previous work, we found that a population of CA1 hippocampal neurons fired in an odor-specific manner during specific epochs of the DNMS task; some fired during the presentation of specific odors (‘odor fields’) and others at timepoints during the delay period (‘time fields’) after presentation of specific odors19. Here, we observed CA1 neurons with activity patterns consistent with BTSP during expert DNMS performance (Fig. 1f-g and Supp. Fig. S1 and S2). Namely, neurons without a clear odor or time field developed a stable field after a single spontaneous large calcium event.

A single somatic calcium ‘reference event’ was considered an induction event if it preceded the formation of an odor-field. Using a set of strict criteria, we labeled every calcium event as succeeding or failing to form an odor-field (see methods). Larger ‘reference event’ amplitudes coincided with higher success rates of odor-field formation (Fig. 1h), indicating that these induction events preceded the formation of odor-fields. Events with amplitudes > 10 standard deviations (STD) of the mean deconvolved signal yielded a significantly asymmetrical field-formation, with the new odor-field occurring earlier in trial-time on subsequent trials compared to the reference event (Fig. 1i); similarly to spatial BTSP in previous studies1–11. We thus considered a reference calcium event as ‘plateau-like’ when its amplitude was > 10 STD.

Plateau-like events were rare (122,605 out of 16,215,467 total events recorded = 0.76%) and matched the shapes and amplitudes of previously described somatic calcium plateau events3,11 (Supp. Fig. S3a-d). Approximately 8% of plateau like events that occurred during the odor cue or within the ensuing 0.5 seconds preceded a subsequent odor-field formation (294 ‘successes’ out of 3876 total events). This increased to ~15% during the second half of the odor presentation cue (Fig. 1j). Only 26 ‘plateau-like’ events beyond 0.5 seconds after odor offset preceded a subsequent time-field formation (8% of the 320 successful events). The odor-fields preceded by plateau-like events peaked 0.42 ± 0.14 seconds earlier in trial-time compared to the reference event (Fig. 1k). In contrast, only 0.28% of ‘small events’ (<10 STD amplitude) during the odor cue or the ensuing 0.5 seconds (254 out of 91,635 total events) preceded new odor fields (Supp. Fig. S5a), These events represent the noise floor of our detection criteria and the rare odor-field formation that formed without a preceding ‘plateau-like’ event. These rare fields were symmetrically distributed around the reference event timepoint with increased variance (Supp. Fig. S5b). We thus label ‘plateau-like’ events preceding an odor-field as ‘BTSP-like’.

We observed no difference in success rates or asymmetrical field-formation between first and second odor (Supp. Fig. S4). Therefore, all odor cues were pooled for further analysis.

Categorizing BTSP-like events into successes and failures restricted analysis to a narrowly defined type of plasticity event based on formation of significant odor responses. Some responses were reinforced by multiple ‘plateau-like’ events (Supp. Fig. S2). Therefore, we developed a simpler analysis to avoid artificially imposed criteria and sensitivity to binary thresholding. Here, we measure potentiation as the increase in firing rate across 10 trials after versus 10 trials before a reference calcium event (‘firing rate increase’). We observed an asymmetrical ramp of firing rate increase with a peak in subsequent trials 0.25 seconds earlier in trial-time than the reference event timepoint (Fig. 1l). No increase was observed when aligned to small events (Fig. 1l). While the firing rate increase was significant up to 3 seconds earlier and 1 second later in trial-time, we focused on the average increase in the 1-second period preceding the reference event. Similar to the previous binary success rate analysis, we found that a significant firing rate increase only occurred after events greater than 8 STD in amplitude (Fig. 1m). This increase was highly odor selective (Fig. 1m). The firing rate increase peaked during the second half of the odor presentation and remained significant up to halfway through the delay (Fig. 1n), suggesting that time-fields during the delay period may form after several successive plateau potentials. Results were similar for a range of trial numbers averaged before and after the reference event (Supp. Fig. S6a-d). Both analysis methods demonstrate that the formation of odor-fields occurred with non-spatial BTSP-like events that are characterized by an asymmetric firing rate increase ramp.

To determine if locomotion influenced non-spatial BTSP-like events, we recorded treadmill locomotion during the task. Mice exhibited a range of locomotion patterns while performing the task with some mice rarely moving on the treadmill, some primarily flinching or twitching at the onset of some odor presentations, and others with bouts of running throughout the trial. On average, minor jitter movements occurred at the onset of 20% of odors and running occurred in up to 5% of trials (Supp. Fig. S7a-b). On average, animals spent 90.4 ± 2.3 % of the time immobile on the treadmill, 7.0 ± 1.7 % of the time with minor jitter movements, and only 2.6 ± 1.8 % of the time running (Supp. Fig. S7c). As expected41–43, movement increased neural activity. Both minor jitter movements and running increased the rate of small events and ‘plateau-like’ events (Supp. Fig. S7d-e). However, neither of these types of movements during reference ‘plateau-like’ events influenced the success rate of field formation or firing rate increase (Supp. Fig. S7f-g). In total, out of the 323 detected successful events, 235 (73%) occurred during periods without movement, 70 (22%) occurred during minor jitter movements, and only 18 (6%) occurred during running bouts. Moreover, mice spent 13.9 ± 4.2 % of time licking (primarily during the reward period of non-match trials) (Supp. Fig S7h-j), which also increased the rate of ‘plateau-like’ events (Supp. Fig. S7k-l). Yet, the success rate and firing rate increase was lower for licking bouts (Supp. Fig. S7m-n). In total, 289 (89%) occurred during periods without licking, and only 34 (11%) occurred during licking bouts. Collectively, our findings reveal formation of odor-specific fields occurred with non-spatial BTSP-like events that were not correlated with locomotion or licking behavior.

Single-neuron holographical optogenetic stimulation induced odor-fields

To confirm that large calcium events causally drive the formation of odor-specific fields, we performed simultaneous two-photon calcium imaging and single-neuron holographic optogenetic stimulation in three animals genetically expressing GCaMP (two mice GCaMP6s and one mouse GCaMP8s). Mice were injected with AAV8-CaMKIIa-ChRmine-mScarlet- Kv2.1-WPRE into the right dorsal CA1 to drive expression of the excitatory opsin ChrRmine in pyramidal neurons (Fig. 2a). To replicate the size and width of spontaneously recorded somatic calcium ‘plateau-like’ events (Supp. Fig. S3a-d), we stimulated individual CA1 neurons of well-trained mice for one second (10ms pulses at 10Hz) at various timepoints throughout the entire trial period from 1st odor presentation to middle of the reward period. After recording at least 4 baseline trials, individual stimulation points were delivered at least 6 seconds apart during task performance. Across multiple days and different FOVs with up to 72 stimulated neurons per day, we successfully induced ‘BTSP-like’ events yielding new stable odor-fields following a single stimulation (Fig. 2b-c). Induced event amplitudes varied in size (likely due to varying levels of ChRmine expression and/or excitability state of the neuron) (Fig. 2d, Supp. Fig. S3e-l), but all successful induction events were greater than 10 STD, validating our previously used criteria. Using these same criteria as above, we isolated stimulation events that were preceded by minimal activity and no significant field (111 out of 857 total stimulations across 16 recording sessions in 3 mice). Stimulation-induced ‘plateau-like’ events during the odor cue or ensuring 0.5 seconds had an 11% probability of odor-field formation (5 out of 44 events), similar to that of spontaneous plateau-like events (~8%). In contrast, stimulation-induced ‘plateau-like’ events outside of this time window (0 out of 33 events), or those with <10 STD amplitude (0 out of 34 stimulation attempts) were not followed by field formation. Importantly, the success rate of field formation and firing rate increase after stimulation (Fig. 2e-f) were similar to the spontaneous events we recorded in Figure 1. Therefore, large somatic plateau-like events causally drive the formation of odor-fields.

Highest rates of non-spatial BTSP occurred early in learning

Given the role of spatial BTSP in formation of place cells during learning of a novel spatial environment, we next asked if non-spatial BTSP-like events were also more frequent earlier in learning of non-spatial cues. To address this question, we repeated two-photon calcium imaging of pyramidal CA1 neurons in five mice during learning of the olfactory DNMS task. To include learning of the odor cues themselves, we introduced them only at the final training stage. Mice were first trained to lick at the appropriate reward window by providing only auditory clicks at the timepoints used for odor onset and offset. This allowed the mice to learn the temporal structure of the task without receiving any odors (Fig. 3a). Mice licked during the reward period for more than 90% of trials during these ‘odor-free’ shaping days. On the following ‘Day 1’, odors were delivered for the first time and mice continued to lick during most trials yielding chance-level performance on Days 1 and 2. By days 3 and 4, mice began refraining from licking on match trials (Fig. 3b) and gradually increased their performance to expert-level (85%) around Day 5 (Fig. 3c). Imaging was conducted on the last two days of ‘odor-free’ shaping (Days -2 and -1), and 9 days during the final stage of the olfactory DNMS task. The same FOV was used on each day for each animal.

Compared to baseline ‘odor-free’ shaping days, the ‘plateau-like’ event rate strongly increased in Day 1 and remained relatively stable across all subsequent days of learning, and with a weak correlation with performance (Fig. 3d, Supp. Table 1). However, the success rate of these ‘plateau-like’ events generating an odor-field peaked on Day 1 compared to the following days and was anti-correlated with performance (Fig. 3e). We used a linear regression model to isolate the relative predictive strength of days of training and behavioral performance on our recorded measures. We found that both were significantly predictive of success rate of ‘plateau-like’ events during the odor period (Days: t = -3.19, p = 0.003; Performance: t = -2.62, p = 0.012; Supp. Table 2). Analysis of the firing rate increase ramps (Fig. 3f) revealed a similar effect when compared across the days of learning for the same odor trials (Days: t = -1.85, p = 0.072; Performance: t = -2.16, p = 0.037; Fig. 3g, Supp. Table 3). Notably, the very small firing rate increase during the opposite odor trials remained stable through all days of baseline and learning trials (Days: t = -0.95, p = 0.35; Performance: t = -0.36, p = 0.72; Fig. 3h, Supp. Table 4), suggesting that these non-specific increases may be due to other factors such as inputs related to auditory clicks rather than odor-specific information. Smaller firing rate increases observed during the delay period also showed a strong negative correlation with performance for same odor trials (Days: t = -5.03, p = 1.0e-05; Performance: t = -4.71, p = 2.8e-05; Fig. 3i, Supp. Table 5). Importantly, minor jitter movements and running did not change significantly across learning (Supp. Fig. 8, Supp. Tables 8-11), thus they cannot account for differences observed across days. Therefore, despite a stable rate of ‘plateau-like’ events during learning, the rate of non-spatial BTSP-like events was highest early in learning of novel odor cues, likely due partially to both novelty and behavioral performance.

Chemogenetic inhibition of entorhinal cortex disrupted non-spatial BTSP

Entorhinal inputs can drive BTSP induction events during spatial learning tasks7,44. To determine whether entorhinal inputs may also play a role in the generation of ‘plateau-like’ events during non-spatial BTSP, we used chemogenetic inhibition of lateral entorhinal cortex (LEC) or medial entorhinal cortex (MEC), while imaging CA1 calcium activity during expert performance of the working memory task. Mice were injected with AAV1-Syn-jGCaMP8f in the dorsal CA1 and were subsequently implanted with an optical canula over CA1 as in the previous section. These mice also received an injection of AAV5-CaMKII-PSAM4 into either LEC (n=6 mice) or MEC (n=5 mice) to express the potent chemogenetic inhibitor PSAM445 in excitatory neurons of either structure (Fig. 4a). Control mice underwent injections of AAV5-CaMKII-mCherry into either LEC (n=3 mice) or MEC (n=3 mice). Animals were water-restricted, trained on the task, and imaged three weeks after viral expression. Each animal was recorded for eight days after reaching expert level performance. Between 10-20 minutes before two-photon calcium imaging began each day, mice received an intraperitoneal (IP) injection of saline or uPSEM (the effector molecule for PSAM4). Saline and uPSEM injections were alternated daily and animals were counter-balanced such that one half of the mice received injections of uPSEM on the first day and the other half received injections of saline. We compared the activity of matched neurons over four pairs of saline and uPSEM days during expert performance when BTSP-like event rates were stable.

Despite a lack of a behavioral effect (Supp. Fig. S9a), both LEC and MEC inhibition strongly affected the non-spatial ‘BTSP-like’ events during expert performance. MEC, but not LEC, inhibition significantly reduced the number of ‘plateau-like’ events from 1.91 ± 0.98 per neuron per day to 1.60 ± 1.12 per neuron per day (Fig. 4b). In contrast, LEC, but not MEC, dramatically reduced the success rate of ‘plateau-like’ events during odor presentations from 7.20 ± 3.61% to 3.18 ± 3.48% (Fig. 4c). Additionally, only LEC inhibition significantly decreased the firing rate increase ramps during the 1-second window preceding reference ‘plateau-like’ events on uPSEM days (Fig. 4d). For ‘plateau-like’ events during odor presentation of LEC PSAM animals, the firing rate increase was significantly lower on uPSEM days for same odor trials but significantly higher for opposite odor trials (Fig. 4e-f). Importantly, neither LEC nor MEC inhibition affected minor jitter movements, running, or licking, so these effects could not be explained by differences in animal movement (Supp. Fig. S9b-e). Together, these findings suggest that MEC plays a role in the large ‘plateau-like’ events in CA1, while LEC activity increases the likelihood that these events result in successful field generation. The differential effects of firing rate increase between same odor and opposite odor trials suggest that LEC inputs to the hippocampus are necessary for relaying odor-specific information.

LEC inhibition reduced strength of odor representations in dorsal CA1

Given that LEC inputs have been previously shown to encode odor-related information31–34, we hypothesized that they could convey odor-related information to CA1 in our DNMS task. If so, we would expect the inhibition of LEC but not MEC to decrease odor-selectivity in CA1, potentially driving the decrease in success rate of ‘plateau-like’ events in generating odor-fields. Indeed, LEC chemogenetic inhibition significantly decreased the percentage of significantly odor-selective neurons from 24.5 ± 9.6% on saline control days and only 16.2 ± 10.8% on uPSEM inhibition days (Fig. 4g), while having no effect on any of the other animal groups. To further confirm this effect, we performed binary support vector machine (SVM) decoding training and testing on the same day to evaluate the relative strength of odor encoding on saline days compared to uPSEM days subsampling only 100 neurons. Overall, LEC inhibition significantly decreased odor decoding accuracy, while MEC inhibition did not alter it (Fig. 4h). While the effect in LEC experimental PSAM4 animals also was observed during the first half of the delay period, the effect during the odor presentation period was the strongest with decoding accuracy at 76.4 ± 10.2% on saline control days and only 66.7 ± 14.3% on uPSEM inhibition days. Odor decoding of MEC experimental PSAM4 and control animals expressing mCherry was unaffected by uPSEM administration. Collectively, LEC inhibition strongly decreased odor-selectivity and decodability in pyramidal CA1 neurons, which may have played a role in the reduction in the success rate of ‘plateau-like’ events in generating odor-fields, though additional mechanisms could potentially contribute to this effect. Additionally, these results are limited to expert performance, so we are unable to determine if these manipulations would affect the previously found novelty and learning results.

Two-photon calcium imaging of temporammonic entorhinal cortical axons in dorsal CA1 revealed differential sequential activity in LEC and MEC inputs

The EC is the primary cortical input to the hippocampus; CA1 receives direct layer III EC input via the temporammonic (TA) pathway and indirect input via the perforant path from layer II EC to dentate gyrus, which then projects to CA3, which in turn projects to CA129,30. Given the contribution of MEC in driving ‘plateau-like’ events, we asked if there are differences in timing of LEC and MEC TA inputs. Also, given the strong differences in odor decodability observed in dorsal CA1 with LEC versus MEC inhibition, we asked whether TA inputs from LEC and MEC differ in the olfactory information they convey to CA1.

To address these questions, we performed two-photon calcium imaging of LEC or MEC TA axons in dorsal CA1 during expert performance of the DNMS task. Adult male and female mice were injected with AAV1-CaMKII-Cre and AAV1-CAG-FLEX-jGCaMP7s in either LEC (n=8) or MEC (n=8) (Fig. 5a,c). Mice were implanted with hippocampal windows as in the previous experiments. After three weeks of expression, there was extensive GCaMP7s axonal expression of TA inputs within the stratum lacunosum-moleculare (SLM) layer, as well as layer II EC perforant path axons ramifying deeper within the stratum moleculare (MOL) layer of the dentate gyrus (Fig. 5a,c). In vivo, we were able to selectively image TA EC axons 300-400 µm beneath the alveus. Post-hoc histology after two-photon imaging experiments also confirmed that all mice had extensive expression of GCaMP7s in axons within the SLM layer of hippocampus and somatic expression restricted to either LEC or MEC. Recordings were processed with Suite2p40 using parameters optimized for axonal imaging, followed by post-hoc fusion of axon segments with highly correlated activity which were branches of the same axon (see methods) (Fig. 5b,d). Only behavioral sessions with expert-performance, with no difference between the groups, were used for the following analysis (Supp. Fig. S10c).

A proportion of LEC and MEC TA axons responded reliably at specific timepoints with some having significant peaks during the odor presentation, some during odor offset, and others during the delay period (Fig. 5e-f). Altogether, the LEC or MEC axonal populations had sequential activity that tiled the entire first odor presentation and delay period. However, these sequences differed drastically between LEC and MEC (Fig. 5g and Supp. Fig. S10a-b). A much higher percentage of MEC axons had significant peaks during odor presentations and their offset compared to LEC axons (MEC with 28.0 ± 6.5% axons with activity peaking during odor presentations compared to only 9.5 ± 6.5% for LEC; MEC with 4.6 ± 2.2% axons with activity peaking during odor offset compared to only 2.7 ± 1.0% for LEC) (Fig. 5h). MEC axons with activity peaking during odor presentations also showed greater trial reliability compared to LEC (Supp. Fig. S10d). In contrast, a higher percentage of LEC axons had significant activity peaks during the delay period (LEC with 5.8 ± 1.3% axons with activity peaking during delay period compared to only 2.4 ± 0.7% for MEC). Given that MEC inhibition reduced the rate of ‘plateau-like’ events in CA1, we hypothesize that this strong MEC input timed to the odor presentation possibly important for driving ‘plateau-like’ events.

LEC temporammonic axonal activity encoded stronger odor-specific information than MEC axonal activity

Although a higher proportion of MEC axons were tuned to firing during the odor presentation, examination of sequential firing patterns suggested that these axons were firing with less odor-specificity (Fig. 5g and Supp. Fig. S10a-b). LEC axons with a significant peak during the odor presentation had larger odor-selectivity values than MEC (LEC with an average of 0.261 ± 0.068 compared to only 0.179 ± 0.033 for MEC) (Fig. 5h). Again, to confirm this difference in odor-selectivity, we performed binary support vector machine (SVM) decoding training and testing on the same day using only the most selective 10 axons from each recording session. First odor decoding accuracy was higher in LEC compared to MEC for both the odor/offset period and the remaining 4 seconds of the delay period (68.4 ± 5.6% for LEC and 62.3 ± 7.2% for MEC during odor/offset 0-2 second window; 61.5 ± 9.5% for LEC and 53.9 ± 3.3% for MEC during odor/offset 2-6 second window). Altogether, these findings suggest that LEC temporammonic axonal odor representations were stronger than MEC axonal odor representations, and this may possibly explain the decrease in success rate and firing rate increases with LEC inhibition, although strong odor information is also likely being relayed indirectly to the CA1 via the perforant path as well.
