Reviewer #2: Summary:
The study by Dorian et al. investigates whether behavioral timescale plasticity (BTSP) can drive the
formation of memory-related non-spatial hippocampal representations. This question is addressed by
performing calcium imaging from hippocampal CA1 cells as well as from LEC and MEC axons in CA1
while mice are performing an olfactory working memory task. In addition, optogenetic induction of
BTSPs in CA1 and chemogenetic manipulations of LEC and MEC are performed to establish that
the success and frequency of BTSPs. Furthermore, recordings during task acquisition show that the
relative frequency of BTSP is increased early in training on the odor task. The series of experiments is
performed with high rigor, and appropriate statistical methods are used. Importantly, the experiments
yield a highly novel result, which is that BTSP is a general plasticity mechanism and not limited to the
formation of spatial fields. In addition to reporting this key result, the study also characterizes some
mechanism of how BTSPs contribute to the encoding of non-spatial representations. As with any
novel phenomenon, the study of course raises a number of interesting questions for future work, such
as the limited effectiveness of BTSPs to generate fields later in the delay. The study is nonetheless
comprehensive as well as exceptional in its impact and novelty. There are only a few minor points
that, if addressed, would further improve the manuscript.
We thank the reviewer for their positive words and careful review of our manuscript. Overall, the
reviewer’s comments led to additional analysis and improved language that contribute to a stronger
manuscript.

(8) In the Results and in the Discussion, it would be more precise to distinguish two potential types of
effects as a consequence of manipulating entorhinal inputs to CA1. One type is plasticity/BTSP-
related, and although detectable in well-trained mice, may no longer be as behaviorally relevant as it
would be if the manipulation were done earlier in training. The second type are effects on
hippocampal activity patterns as a consequence of loss of information from LEC or MEC. With any
manipulation of a brain region, effects on plasticity and from loss of inputs to connected circuits can
often not be fully dissociated. It is nonetheless important to conceptually distinguish between these
types of effects and to acknowledge that both contribute to differences in neuronal firing patterns
during/after manipulations.
We now discuss the difficulty of teasing these two potential effects apart in the Results:
“Collectively, LEC inhibition strongly decreased odor-selectivity and decodability in pyramidal CA1
neurons, which may have played a role in the reduction in the success rate of ‘plateau-like’ events in
generating odor-fields, though additional mechanisms could potentially contribute to this effect.
Additionally, these results are limited to expert performance, so we are unable to determine if these
manipulations would affect the previously found novelty and learning results.”
We discuss it in more detail in the Discussion:
“First, it is important to note that we only observed these effects in expert-performance. Perhaps the
effects that we observed in expert animals would become behaviorally relevant during early training.
Alternatively, the loss of information from LEC or MEC may affect CA1 activity regardless of the stage
of behavioral performance. Future experiments will be necessary to tease apart these possibilities.”

We thank Reviewer #1 for their additional constructive feedback and acknowledgement of our
“detailed rebuttal and substantial revisions”. We have updated the manuscript and addressed all
concerns in the point-by-point discussion below.
Reviewer #1:
Thank you for the detailed rebuttal and substantial revisions. Several of my earlier concerns are now
at least partially addressed, especially the change in terminology to “plateau-like” events, the added
discussion of somatic imaging caveats, and the corrections to error bars. However, I still feel that the
strength and scope of the main claims exceed what the data can support, and I would strongly
encourage further tempering of the mechanistic and causal language, as well as clearer
acknowledgment of alternative interpretations.
We thank the reviewer for their thoughtful feedback. We have now addressed these concerns
by improving our statistical tests and further tempering mechanistic and causal language while more
clearly discussing alternative interpretations of our results.
Mechanistic and causal claims
While the authors have removed some explicit causal phrases and now refer to “plateau-like” rather
than “BTSP-like” events, the title, abstract, and discussion still largely present the results as
demonstrating that BTSP is a general plasticity mechanism for non-spatial representations. In
particular, the concluding statement in the abstract that the findings “demonstrate a causal role of
BTSP” is not supported by the present data. Given that all inferences are based on somatic calcium
signals and an operational definition of ≥10 SD events, this remains too strong. The same somatic
signature could arise from different underlying mechanisms (e.g. bursts, mixed dendritic/somatic
events), and the data demonstrate correlation and temporal precedence rather than necessity or
sufficiency. I would recommend consistently rephrasing to something more neutral, such as “rare,
large somatic calcium events consistent with BTSP models can precede the formation of some odor
fields in this task,” and avoiding language that implies that BTSP per se has been established as the
mechanism.
We have made several changes to address these concerns.
First, we have changed the Title to read: “Rapid formation of non-spatial hippocampal
representations consistent with behavioral timescale synaptic plasticity is modulated by entorhinal
input”
Second, we have changed the concluding sentence in the Abstract to read: “Together, our
findings demonstrate that rare large somatic calcium events, consistent with BTSP, precede and drive
novel odor representations during learning, in a manner differentially regulated by medial and lateral
entorhinal cortex.”
Third, to be consistent with this new language, we have also adjusted similar summarizing
sentences in the Discussion.
Last, while we agree that tempering claims is appropriate in regard to the mechanism
underlying the formation of odor representations, we would like to point out that experimental results
shown in Figure 2 suggest sufficiency since we were able to optogenetically-induce odor
representations with somatic excitation. We now acknowledge that BTSP is likely just one of several
mechanisms potentially driving formation of hippocampal representations. Furthermore, we now more
fully discuss the difficult problem of testing necessity of BTSP in the Discussion.
The revised text better documents numerators/denominators and threshold choices, but the core
concern about circularity remains. “Possible induction events” are defined using stringent criteria (low
prior activity, no strong field in the preceding trials, restricted trial window), and “success” is then
defined as a new, reliable field emerging near the event in time. This effectively preselects events in
which a silent-to-active transition occurs with the desired temporal asymmetry and discards cases
where fields emerge more gradually, overlap existing activity, or arise without a qualifying event. The
binary analysis therefore builds the BTSP-like pattern into the inclusion criteria and will, by
construction, emphasize one-shot, asymmetric field formation. The more continuous “threshold-free”
analysis is a welcome addition, but the manuscript should more clearly acknowledge that the
binary/“induction” analysis is conditional on these strong filters and cannot be taken as an unbiased
estimate of how often plateau-like events genuinely drive fields versus other scenarios.
We have now further revised the text to emphasize the differences between the two types of
analysis. In the Results (page 4), it now reads “Categorizing BTSP-like events into successes and
failures restricted analysis to a narrowly defined type of plasticity event based on formation of
significant odor responses. Some responses were reinforced by multiple ‘plateau-like’ events (Supp.
Fig. S2). Therefore, we developed a simpler analysis to avoid artificially imposed criteria and
sensitivity to binary thresholding.”
In the Discussion, it now reads “analysis that binarizes complex dynamics into successes and
failures is sensitive to chosen thresholds, and this makes it inherently difficult to compare across
contexts and recording methods. Similar discrepancies can even be seen within spatial tasks, as the
reported percentages of CA1 pyramidal neurons that are classified as place cells can vary
dramatically between 20% and 90%50. Therefore, our reported values for BTSP success cannot be
extrapolated to BTSP rates beyond our experimental and analytical parameters. For this reason, we
also developed and utilized the threshold-free analysis of firing rate increase.”
As before, we argue that the binary analysis is still useful because of its widespread use in
spatial BTSP research classifying the formation of place fields, but we have now tempered our
explanations in the Results and Discussion.
Generality and time representations
The manuscript still suggests that BTSP underlies non-spatial representations more broadly, including
time. However, the data show that only a very small minority of plateau-like events occurring after
odor offset precede time fields, and optogenetic induction in the delay period did not reliably generate
fields. The discussion now notes that delay-related effects are weaker and rare, but the claims about
generalization to time and “internally generated” codes still read as if they are an established
extension of the mechanism rather than an open question. I would recommend explicitly stating that
the present data provide only limited support for BTSP-like contributions to time fields and that the
role of such events in temporal coding remains unresolved.
We agree with the reviewer. The noted section in the Discussion now reads “Although we
observed small firing rate increases and rare BTSP-like events that form odor-specific fields during
the delay period, our findings only provide limited support of BTSP-like events contributing to
temporal coding. Future studies should investigate if recurrent CA3 networks capable of generating
temporal codes55–57 can be activated coincidentally with LEC and MEC to drive BTSP for internally
generated representations.”
Behavioral relevance and EC silencing

This is now documented more clearly, but the manuscript still leans toward a causal interpretation in
which BTSP-dependent representations are central for task solution. Given the lack of behavioral
effect in the regime actually recorded, a more balanced formulation would be that LEC and MEC
manipulations alter neural representations and event statistics during expert performance, but their
necessity for behavior under these conditions is not demonstrated. Any stronger inference about
“BTSP creating behaviorally relevant representations” should be softened accordingly or explicitly
framed as a hypothesis for future work (e.g. during acquisition or more demanding variants of the
task).
We have removed statements that mention ‘behavioral relevance’ in the Results and
Discussion. Additionally, we have expanded the section in the Discussion to further discuss this
important idea: “Perhaps the effects that we observed in expert animals would be stronger if tested
during early training. Alternatively, the loss of information from LEC or MEC may affect CA1 activity
regardless of the stage of behavioral performance. Furthermore, the lack of behavioral performance
deficits with either LEC or MEC inhibition suggests that these representations are not necessary for
the performance of this specific task. Future experiments with inhibition at different stages of learning
and across various tasks will be necessary to isolate the behavioral relevance of LEC and MEC
inputs driving BTSP-like events in CA1.”
Statistical issues
- The authors state that they now use linear regression to separate day and performance, and
they have corrected the chemogenetic error bars, which is appreciated. Nonetheless, several
statistical concerns remain:
- Regression analyses treat each animal–day as an independent data point without modeling
mouse as a random effect. With only five mice followed over multiple days, this violates the
hierarchical structure of the data and likely underestimates uncertainty on day/performance
effects.
We thank the reviewer for pointing out this error and have now updated all regression figures,
statistics, and supplemental tables after modeling mouse as a random effect (slope and intercept).
This approach is better suited to repeated measurements for each mouse, better captures animal
variability, has more power, and thus strengthens our findings. All corresponding figure panels now
display larger t-values and smaller p-values, including ‘Plateau-like’ Event Rate in Figure 3D which
is now significant but weaker than all other effects. We now note this difference in the text.
Supplemental Tables contain all MATLAB Table outputs regarding the model and results.
- Event-level analyses still appear to treat individual events as independent observations in
some tests, even though many events come from the same cells and animals, again inflating
effective n and p-values.
The reviewer’s point applies to Figures 1K and 2D depicting histograms for visualization. All
statistics and other figure panels are performed on animal averages or session averages. We
denote this in the legend text with statements such as “Individual thin gray lines represent each of
the 17 animals (which are the average for each of their 8 recording sessions)”. The only other use
of individual events is when we summarize total counts in the main text (e.g. “294 ‘successes’ out
of 3876 total events”), which are summary quantifications without statistics involved.
- The multi-factor ANOVAs in the chemogenetic experiments are based on very small group
sizes (e.g. n = 3 controls), where parametric assumptions are fragile and effect sizes or
confidence intervals would be more informative than marginal p-values.

statistics.
We appreciate this suggestion. In each figure legend corresponding to figure panels with three-way
ANOVAs we have now included the 95% confidence interval for each significant difference. This is
included for Figure 4B, 4C, 4E, 4F, 4G, 4I, and Supplementary Figure S6I.
Context from Sumegi et al.
The authors now cite Sumegi et al. as using somatic calcium to study BTSP-like phenomena.
Importantly, that work also shows that large somatic Ca² events with BTSP-like signatures are
neither necessary nor sufficient for place field formation and that diverse calcium dynamics can
underlie new fields. This does not contradict the present ⁺study, but it reinforces the idea that large
somatic “plateau-like” events are one of several possible routes to field formation. In my view, this
makes it even more important that the current manuscript frame its main conclusion as the
identification of one correlated pathway in a specific non-spatial task, rather than as establishing
BTSP as the general mechanism for non-spatial representations.
We have edited the first summary paragraph of the Discussion to read “These events are
consistent with models of behavioral timescale synaptic plasticity (BTSP), as they demonstrate
asymmetrical formation observed previously during spatial tasks1–11. This suggests that BTSP may be
one plasticity mechanism capable of driving rapid formation of hippocampal representations during
both spatial and non-spatial cognition.”
Additionally, we have expanded a section to discuss the diversity of calcium events as seen in
Sumegi et al. It now reads “Additionally, alternative mechanisms may also play a role, consistent with
recent research demonstrating a variety of somatic calcium dynamics preceding formation of place
fields51. Indeed, the rapid formation of odor responses after optogenetically-induced somatic plateau-
like events suggests sufficiency, but the low success rate suggests other mechanisms could also be
involved. Furthermore, tests of necessity are difficult due to our present limited knowledge of the
mechanisms underlying BTSP.”
In summary, the additional analyses and revisions improve the manuscript, but I still recommend a
further toning down of mechanistic and causal language, more explicit discussion of alternative
mechanisms and the limitations of the operational definition, clearer acknowledgment of the lack of
behavioral impact of EC silencing under the conditions tested, and a more cautious treatment of
generalization to time fields.
We thank the reviewer for their suggestions. We have addressed each of these concerns with
revisions of text throughout the Abstract, Results, and Discussion sections.
